bible_refs.note: συνήγειρεν καὶ συνεκάθισεν ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις; Cyril in the passive, first person.
ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη … καταργηθῇ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας.
Lemma, given short and then in full.
Buried with him through baptism (συντεθάφθαι); Colossians 2:12 is parallel.
Dead to sin, alive to God.
Full quotation; Cyril reads ὅπλα and εἰς τὸ ὑπακούειν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις αὐτοῦ.
ἡ τοῦ νόμου σκιά: Cyril's stock phrase from σκιὰν γὰρ ἔχων ὁ νόμος (Hebrews 10:1; compare Colossians 2:17). Added inline by the independent review.

choices.why: παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος rendered “old self” for readability; Cyril means the earthly body bearing the ancient corruption from Adam (see u03-rem-early).
κέντρον τῆς ἁμαρτίας: “sting of sin”; a possible echo of 1 Corinthians 15:56, not cited inline because the wording differs.
πνευματοφόρος (“the Spirit-bearer”) is Paul; Spirit capitalised as the Holy Spirit.
ὑποτρέχειν τὴν ἐν Χριστῷ χάριν: “take shelter under” the grace, keeping the image of running under cover set against the law’s shadow.

pass_a_gloss: [καθάπερ] indeed also in Adam, when he became accursed (ἐπάρατος), the whole nature (φύσις) fell sick with the curse (ἀρά); for thus also we are said to have been co-raised (συνεγηγέρθαι) with Christ and to co-sit in the heavenlies; for even if Emmanuel is above us as God, yet since he became according to us as one of us, he has been raised and sits together with the God and Father. Was co-crucified (συνεσταυρώθη) therefore the old man (παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος); for loosed through the resurrection is the power of that ancient curse; abolished (κατήργηται) also the body of sin (σῶμα τῆς ἁμαρτίας), and not at all the flesh (σάρξ), but of the motions (κινήματα) in it the inborn (ἔμφυτος) savagery (ἀγριότης), shaking down always toward the more shameful the mind (νοῦς), plunging as into mud and swamps of the more earthy pleasures (ἡδοναί). That in Christ this too has been set right for human nature, how would one doubt, Paul saying clearly [Romans 8:3]? Do you see how the body of sin has been abolished? Condemned (κατακέκριται) in the flesh is the goad (κέντρον) of sin; and it was deadened in Christ first, and passed from him and through him also into us the grace (χάρις). [Lemma Romans 7:1] Everywhere he declares unsafe (ἐπισφαλές) the seeking to lie under law; urges rather to desire and with whole mind to thirst for the grace through faith (πίστις), that is the justification (δικαίωσις) in Christ; with whom he insisted the baptized were co-buried, so that deadened to sin they might live to God in righteousness. Therefore he said [Romans 6:12-14]. Look how he orders to depart from the shadow (σκιά) of the law, to run under rather the grace in Christ. But the Spirit-bearer (πνευματοφόρος) did not fail to know that some will surely say, or reason, that the fathers then missed the straight road and life; the law profited them nothing, and gone somehow already the boasts (αὐχήματα) of their polity (πολιτεία). For if it is among absurd things to seek to lie under law, and this was for the ancients the aim of life, how not true to say they missed the fitting? Contends therefore the one having Christ in himself; and feigns cleverly wishing to speak in support of those who lived under law, but turns them variously toward thinking it needful, the time (καιρός) calling to faith, not much to wish to linger in ancient customs (ἔθη). Thus he says [Romans 7:1 with 'that the law lords over the man as long as he lives']. Definition (ὅρος) this, general, regarding both law…
pass_b_english: …just as in Adam too, when he came under the curse, the whole of human nature fell sick with that curse.
So too we are said to have been raised with Christ and to be seated with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6).
For even though Emmanuel is above us as God, yet since he became like us as one of us, he has been raised and sits beside God the Father.
So our old self was crucified with him (Romans 6:6), for through the resurrection the power of that ancient curse has been broken.

The body of sin has also been done away with (Romans 6:6). This does not mean the flesh itself, but the inborn savagery of the impulses within it, which always drags the mind down toward what is more shameful and sinks it, as it were, into the mud and marshes of earthier pleasures.

That this too has been accomplished for human nature in Christ, who could doubt, when Paul says plainly, “For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans 8:3)?

Do you see, then, how the body of sin has been done away with? For the sting of sin has been condemned in the flesh. It was put to death first in Christ, and the grace has passed from him and through him to us as well.
“Or do you not know, brothers—for I am speaking to those who know the law…” (Romans 7:1).
Everywhere he shows that to seek to be under the law is dangerous.

He urges us rather to long for, and with our whole mind to thirst after, the grace that comes through faith, that is, justification in Christ. He firmly declared that the baptized have been buried with Christ (Romans 6:4), so that, having been put to death to sin, they might live to God in righteousness (Romans 6:11).

That is why he said, “So do not let sin reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its desires. Do not present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members to God as weapons of righteousness. For sin will no longer have dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:12–14).
See, then, how he commands them to leave the shadow of the law (Hebrews 10:1) and instead to take shelter under the grace that is in Christ.

Yet the Spirit-bearer was well aware that some would surely say, or at least reason to themselves, that in that case the fathers had strayed from the straight road and from life, that the law had done them no good, and that the glories of their way of life had somehow already come to nothing.
For if it is absurd to seek to be under the law, and this was the aim of life for the people of old, how could it not be true to say that they missed what was fitting?

So he who has Christ within him takes up the contest. He skilfully gives the impression that he wishes to speak on behalf of those who lived under the law, but in many ways he turns the argument toward the view that, when the time calls to faith, one must not be too eager to linger over the ancient customs.
This is why he says, “Or do you not know, brothers, for I am speaking to those who know the law, that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives?” (Romans 7:1).
This is a general rule, holding both for…

reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Staged row fixed in place in tr1.json. Every clause checked against the source. (1) Title 'The Old Self Crucified' nearly repeated the previous row's title; now 'The Body of Sin Done Away', which names this row's main thought. (2) κατακέκριται γάρ: the 'for' was dropped; restored ('For the sting of sin…'). (3) The short Romans 7:1 lemma was closed as a complete quotation; it breaks off in Greek, so now marked with a dash and ellipsis. (4) τὸ ὑπὸ νόμῳ κεῖσθαι ζητεῖν, twice: 'seek to remain under the law' assumed they were already under it; now 'seek to be under the law'. (5) Romans 6:12 'Let not sin therefore reign' was archaic word order; now 'So do not let sin reign'. (6) τῆς τοῦ νόμου σκιᾶς is a clear allusion to Hebrews 10:1 (σκιὰν γὰρ ἔχων ὁ νόμος); cited inline and added to bible_refs. (7) διημαρτήκασιν ἄρα … οἱ πατέρες: 'had then strayed' read like a time word; ἄρα is inferential, so now 'in that case the fathers had strayed'. (8) περιτρέπει δὲ ποικίλως … καιροῦ καλοῦντος εἰς πίστιν: the English supplied 'them' twice, which pointed back to the dead under the law; the Greek has no object, so now 'he turns the argument toward the view that, when the time calls to faith, one must not…'. Speaker check: the objection is Paul's imagined critics reported by Cyril; the Spirit-bearer is Paul; Emmanuel above us as God, and sits with God the Father, kept exactly.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The row opens mid-sentence: καθάπερ closes the previous row (u03-rem-early), so the English opens with an ellipsis. It also ends mid-sentence (ὅρος οὗτος γενικὸς κατά τε νόμου); the sentence continues in u03-rem-close.
παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος rendered “old self” for readability; Cyril means the earthly body bearing the ancient corruption from Adam (see u03-rem-early).
κέντρον τῆς ἁμαρτίας: “sting of sin”; a possible echo of 1 Corinthians 15:56, not cited inline because the wording differs.
Romans 8:3 kept in its elliptical Greek shape (“what was impossible for the law … God … condemned sin”) without supplying “God did”.
πνευματοφόρος (“the Spirit-bearer”) is Paul; Spirit capitalised as the Holy Spirit.
ὑποτρέχειν τὴν ἐν Χριστῷ χάριν: “take shelter under” the grace, keeping the image of running under cover set against the law’s shadow.
Possible echo of Genesis 3:17 (the curse in Adam) not cited inline; Cyril does not quote it.
